guide.what: Articles are the little words before a noun: el, la, los, las (the) and un, una, unos, unas (a, some). In Spanish they must match the noun in gender (masculine/feminine) and number (singular/plural).

rules.d: Pick the article by the gender and number of the noun: el/la, los/las, un/una, unos/unas. Learn every new noun together with its article.
rules.ex: el carro, la casa, los carros, las casas
rules.exEn: the car, the house, the cars, the houses

rules.d: When you talk about something in general (all coffee, people in general), Spanish uses the definite article. English uses no article.
rules.ex: Me gusta el café, pero no me gustan los dulces.
rules.exEn: I like coffee, but I don't like sweets.

rules.t: Titles, days and time take the article
rules.d: Use the article with titles when you talk about someone (el señor López, la doctora Ruiz), but not when you speak to them. Days: el lunes = on Monday. Time: Son las tres. Dates: el 3 de noviembre.
rules.ex: La doctora Ruiz llega el lunes a las ocho.
rules.exEn: Dr. Ruiz arrives on Monday at eight.

rules.t: Body parts and clothes: article, not 'my'
rules.d: When it's clear whose it is, Spanish uses el/la instead of mi/tu, often with a pronoun like me or se.
rules.ex: Me lavo las manos. Ponte la camisa.
rules.exEn: I wash my hands. Put on your shirt.

rules.d: Use el with a language as a topic (El español es fácil). After hablar, estudiar, aprender, saber and after en, the article is usually dropped.
rules.ex: Hablo español, pero el inglés es mi primer idioma.
rules.exEn: I speak Spanish, but English is my first language.

rules.d: After ser with a profession, nationality or religion, no un/una: Soy profesor. Also no un/una before otro, cierto, medio, tal, or after qué in exclamations. Add un/una only if there is an adjective: Es un buen médico.
rules.ex: Mi esposa es enfermera y quiere otro trabajo.
rules.exEn: My wife is a nurse and wants another job.

rules.t: El and un before stressed a-
rules.d: Feminine nouns beginning with a stressed a- or ha- use el and un in the singular (el agua, un hacha). The noun is still feminine: el agua fría, las aguas.
rules.ex: El agua del río está muy fría.
rules.exEn: The river water is very cold.

rules.d: Lo is a neuter article for ideas, never before a noun. Lo + adjective = the ... thing/part (lo bueno, lo difícil). Lo que = what, the thing that.
rules.ex: Lo difícil es empezar. Eso es lo que quiero.
rules.exEn: The hard part is starting. That's what I want.

rules.d: A + el = al; de + el = del, always. Exceptions: él (de él) and names with El (de El Salvador). Unos/unas = some, a few; before numbers, about.
rules.ex: Voy al banco del centro con unos veinte dólares.
rules.exEn: I'm going to the downtown bank with about twenty dollars.

mistakes.why: No un/una with professions after ser unless there's an adjective.

mistakes.wrong: Café es bueno para la salud.
mistakes.right: El café es bueno para la salud.
mistakes.why: General statements need the definite article.
A + el always contracts to al.
Feminine nouns with stressed a- take el in the singular.
With body parts, use the article, not the possessive.

items.use: Use before masculine singular nouns. Spanish uses it more than English: general statements (el café), titles (el señor López), days (el lunes). No accent: él with accent means 'he'.
items.ex: El carro de mi hermano es nuevo.

items.use: Use before feminine singular nouns. Also for time (la una) and body parts instead of 'my/your' (me duele la cabeza).
Use before masculine plural nouns, or a mix of masculine and feminine. Los + day = every (los lunes = on Mondays).
items.exEn: On Mondays I go to the gym.

items.use: Use before feminine plural nouns. For telling time from two o'clock on: son las tres.
items.ex: Son las tres de la tarde.

items.use: Before masculine singular nouns. Not used with professions after ser (Soy profesor) or before otro, cierto, medio. Un can also mean 'one'.
De + el must join as del. Do not join it with él (de él) or with a name that includes El (de El Salvador). No contraction with la, los, las.
Before feminine singular nouns. Changes to un before a noun starting with stressed a- (un águila), but stays una before an adjective (una gran águila).
items.exEn: I live in a small house.

items.use: A + el must join as al. Not with él or names with El (a El Salvador). Al + infinitive = when/upon doing something.
items.exEn: We're going to the movies tonight.

items.use: Lo + masculine singular adjective = the abstract idea: lo bueno (the good thing), lo importante. Lo que = what, the thing that. Never before a noun.
items.ex: Lo bueno es que no llovió.
items.exEn: The good thing is that it didn't rain.

items.use: Plural of un: some, a few. Before a number it means 'about' (unos veinte). Often left out in English and also in Spanish when vague.
items.ex: Llegaron unos amigos de mi hermano.
items.exEn: Some friends of my brother's arrived.

items.use: Plural of una. Before a number it means 'approximately'. Also 'a pair of' for things in pairs (unas tijeras).
items.ex: Tardé unas dos horas en llegar.
items.exEn: It took me about two hours to get there.

items.en: the, before feminine nouns with stressed a-/ha-
items.use: Feminine nouns that begin with a stressed a- or ha- take el in the singular to avoid 'la a' (el agua, el hacha, el águila). The noun stays feminine: el agua fría, las aguas.

items.en: a, an, before feminine nouns with stressed a-/ha-
items.use: Same rule as el: un hacha, un águila, un aula. The noun is still feminine, so adjectives are feminine and the plural is unas.
items.ex: Mi hijo estudia en un aula muy pequeña.
items.exEn: My son studies in a very small classroom.
